# Essential yet limited role for CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes during Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific T cell priming

## Authors

- Miriam Samstein<sup>1</sup> †
- Heidi A Schreiber<sup>4</sup>
- Ingrid M Leiner<sup>1</sup>
- Bože Sušac<sup>1</sup>
- Michael S Glickman<sup>1</sup>
- Eric G Pamer<sup>1</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. Program in Immunology and Microbial Pathogenesis Weill Cornell Graduate School of Medical Sciences New York United States
2. Infectious Disease Service, Department of Medicine Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center New York United States
3. Weill Cornell, Rockefeller, Sloan-Kettering Tri-Institutional MD-PhD Program New York United States
4. Laboratory of Molecular Immunology The Rockefeller University New York United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Defense against infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is mediated by CD4 T cells. CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes (IMs) have been implicated in Mtb-specific CD4 T cell responses but their in vivo contribution remains unresolved. Herein, we show that transient ablation of IMs during infection prevents Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes, reducing CD4 T cell responses. Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients, while restoring Mtb transport to mLNs, does not enable Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming. On the other hand, transfer of MHC class II-deficient IMs corrects CD4 T cell priming in monocyte-depleted, MHC class II-expressing mice. Specific depletion of classical DCs does not reduce Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes but markedly reduces CD4 T cell priming. Thus, although IMs acquire characteristics of DCs while delivering Mtb to lymph nodes, cDCs but not moDCs induce proliferation of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.

## Introduction

Inflammatory monocytes (IMs) express Ly6c, CD11b and CCR2, a chemokine receptor that facilitates emigration of IMs from the bone marrow (Serbina and Pamer, 2006). Although IMs make important contributions to innate immune defense during infection, recent studies also implicate IMs in priming of CD4 T cell responses during fungal, viral and parasitic infections (Traynor et al., 2000; Leon et al., 2007; Edismo et al., 2009; Hohl et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011). Experiments using CCR2-deficient mice also suggested that monocytes contribute to T-cell-mediated defense against Mtb. IMs, however, can also serve as permissive host cells for Mtb in later stages of infection, suggesting that IMs can both restrict and enhance Mtb infection (Antonelli et al., 2010). Because recruitment of IMs in CCR2-deficient mice is defective throughout early, intermediate and late stages of infection, it has not been possible to specifically define the role of monocytes at different times during infection (Peters et al., 2001; Scott and Flynn, 2002; Peters et al., 2004). Therefore, we used CCR2-DTR mice to transiently deplete IMs and other CCR2-expressing cells during discrete stages of Mtb infection.

## Results and discussion

Administration of DT to these mice depletes inflammatory monocytes from the lung and mLN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). CCR2-DTR mice that received three doses of DT surrounding the time of aerosol infection did not differ from control mice in terms of mycobacterial growth in the lungs (Figure 1A), indicating that CCR2-expressing cells are not required for the establishment of pulmonary infection following Mtb inhalation. Previous studies have demonstrated that CD4 T-cell priming occurs approximately 7–10 days following inhalational challenge (Wolf et al., 2007; Gallegos et al., 2008). Depletion of CCR2-expressing cells 7, 9 and 11 days following infection resulted in a threefold increase in the number of live Mtb in the lungs on day 15 (Figure 1B). To further investigate this finding, we depleted monocytes 7–11 days following infection and quantitatively cultured Mtb from lungs and lymph nodes 12 days following infection. Although monocyte-depleted and control mice had similar Mtb CFUs in lungs at this time (Figure 1C), Mtb CFUs were markedly reduced in mLNs of mice treated with DT (1D).

![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig1-v1.jpg)

**Figure 1.:** (A) CFU plots from the lungs of CCR2-DTR mice receiving DT or PBS on days −1, 0 and 1 and harvested on day 7. (B) CFU plots of the lungs of CCR2-DTR mice receiving DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11 and harvested on day 15 post infection. CFU counts from the lungs (C) and mLN (D) of CCR2-DTR mice given DT treatment on days 7, 9 and 11 and harvested on day 12. Each dot represents an individual mouse. Error bars denote SEM. Data are representative of two independent experiments.

![Figure 1—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig1-figsupp1-v1.jpg)

**Figure 1—figure supplement 1.:** CCR2-DTR mice received PBS or DT on days 7, 9 and 11 post infection and were harvested on day 12 when flow cytometry was performed to quantify the IM population in the lungs (A) and mLN (B). Data are representative of three independent experiments.

We reasoned that reducing live M. tuberculosis transport from the lung to the draining lymph node following monocyte depletion on days 7–11 post infection might delay priming of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells. To address this, we adoptively transferred naïve, Thy1.1-marked, ESAT-6-specific CD4 T cells (C7 T cells) into CCR2-DTR mice prior to aerosol Mtb infection (Gallegos et al., 2008). Monocytes were depleted 7–11 days following infection, and mediastinal lymph nodes and lungs were harvested 12 and 21 days following infection. In comparison to mLNs obtained from PBS treated mice, mLNs obtained from monocyte-depleted mice were smaller, with significantly reduced total and CD4 T cell numbers (Figure 2A). C7 T cells had proliferated in mLNs of control mice 12 days after infection but had not expanded in monocyte-depleted mice (Figure 2B,D). Reduced C7 T cell proliferation in mLNs resulted in reduced C7 T cell frequencies in lungs of monocyte-depleted mice 21 days following infection (Figure 2C,D). Transfer of naïve C7 T cells to control mice resulted in a four to fivefold reduction of Mtb CFUs in lungs, suggesting that supplementing the endogenous T cell repertoire with additional naive, ESAT-6-specific CD4 T cells enhances immune defense against Mtb infection (Figure 2E). Depletion of monocytes abrogated enhanced protection resulting from addition of naive C7 T cells (Figure 2E).

![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig2-v1.jpg)

**Figure 2.:** (A) Total cell counts and CD4 T cell counts in mLNs of mice on day 12 post infection after treatment with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11. CCR2-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11, mLNs (B) were harvested on day 12, lungs (C) were harvested on day 21 and ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells were visualized. (D) Cumulative data from experiments shown in (B) and (C) showing the total number of ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in mLNs and lungs. (E) CFU plots of lungs of mice that received naive EAST-6-specific C7 T cells and were treated with DT or PBS, as indicated, and were harvested on day 21 post infection. Each dot represents an individual mouse. Five mice per group are included in the bar graphs shown in (A). Error bars denote SEM. Data are representative of three independent experiments.

Although IMs represent the most prevalent CCR2-expressing cell population, subsets of NK cells, dendritic cells and CD4 T cells can also express CCR2. To exclude the possibility that depletion of a non-monocyte cell population resulted in loss of Mtb transport from lungs to mLNs, we purified IMs from CCR2-GFP mice by sorting GFP+ cells that did not express NK1.1, CD4, FLT3 and C-kit. This strategy did not require antibody staining for trafficking molecules (CCR2 and CD11b) and eliminated NK cells, CD4 T cells, dendritic cell progenitors and hematopoietic stem cells, yielding a highly purified (>99% pure) population of IMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). We adoptively transferred 2 × 106 IMs on day 8 and 10 of infection while depleting CCR2+ cells on days 7, 9 and 11. The transferred IMs were detectable in lungs and mLNs and down-regulated expression of CCR2 and CD11b and up-regulated expression of MHC class II, CD11c and CD103 during trafficking from the lung to mLNs (Figure 3A,B). Administration of IMs to monocyte-depleted CCR2-DTR mice enhanced live Mtb transport to mLNs, as detected 12 days following infection (Figure 3C). Infusion of IMs to WT mice did not enhance delivery of Mtb to mLNs, suggesting that IMs are not limiting during the first 2 weeks of Mtb infection. Adoptive transfer of IMs to monocyte-depleted CCR2-DTR recipient mice rescued priming of C7 T cells (Figure 3D,E).

![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig3-v1.jpg)

**Figure 3.:** CCR2-DTR mice were infected and treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11 and received highly purified CD45.1+ IMs on days 8 and 10. (A) Mice were euthanized on day 12 post infection and flow cytometry was performed on lungs and mLNs to track the engraftment of adoptively transferred IMs. (B) The expression of cell surface markers CD11b, MHC II, CDIIc and CD103 by adoptively transferred IMs in the lung and mLN was determined. (C) CFU plots from day 12 mLNs of CCR2-DTR mice rescued with IMs. Dots marked in red represent mice that received double sorted IMs of greater than 99% purity. (D) CCR2-DTR mice received a dose of naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT on days 7, 9 and 11 and received purified IMs or PBS on days 8 and 10. Lungs were harvested on day 15 and ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells were visualized. (E) Cumulative data of experiment shown in (D) showing the total number of ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in day 15 lungs. (F) CCR2-DTR mice were depleted on days 7, 9 and 11 and received CCR2 WT or CCR2 KO IMs on days 8 and 10. Day 12 mLNs were harvested for CFU counts. Each dot represents an individual mouse. Error bars denote SEM. Data are representative of two independent experiments.

![Figure 3—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig3-figsupp1-v1.jpg)

**Figure 3—figure supplement 1.:** FACS plots show pre- and post sorting purity of the cells. Data are representative of two independent experiments.

While the CCR2 chemokine receptor is required for egress of IMs from bone marrow (Serbina and Pamer, 2006), the role of CCR2 in trafficking of IMs into infected lungs or from the sites of lung infection to draining lymph nodes remains incompletely resolved. To determine whether CCR2 is required for trafficking to lungs and mLNs during Mtb infection, we purified IMs from CCR2-deficient, CCR2-GFP mice for adoptive transfer into Mtb-infected, CCR2-DTR recipient mice that were monocyte depleted between 7 and 11 days following infection. Quantitative culture 12 days following Mtb infection demonstrated that wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs, indicating that CCR2-signaling does not contribute to trafficking of IMs between these sites (Figure 3F).

Although IMs acquired characteristics of dendritic cells and are essential for Mtb transport from infected lungs to mLNs, it remained unclear whether IMs directly primed Mtb-specific CD4 T cells. Therefore, we transferred C7 T cells into MHC class II-deficient CCR2-DTR mice, depleted monocytes 7–11 days following infection and adoptively transferred MHC class II-expressing purified monocytes on days 8 and 10 following infection. In contrast to our previous experiments with MHC class II-expressing recipients, C7 T cells were not primed in MHC class II-deficient recipients of MHC class II-expressing monocytes (Figure 4A). Adoptively transferred IMs trafficked to mLNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and, as demonstrated in the previous experiments, corrected Mtb delivery to draining lymph nodes to levels seen in mice that had not been monocyte-depleted (Figure 4B). Thus, defective antigen transport to the draining mLN could not explain the lack of CD4 T cell proliferation. In a reciprocal experiment, we transferred MHC class II-deficient IMs into Mtb-infected, MHC class II-expressing CCR2-DTR mice on the same schedule described above and quantified the C7 T cell response. Figure 4C demonstrates that the magnitude of the C7 T cell response was similar in monocyte-depleted mice rescued with either MHC class II-expressing or deficient monocytes. Taken together, these experiments indicate that IMs primarily serve as carriers of Mtb, delivering live bacteria to mLNs and enabling but not directly priming CD4 T cells.

![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig4-v1.jpg)

**Figure 4.:** CCR2-DTR mice that were either MHC class II KO or WT received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11 and received purified IMs on days 8 and 10. (A) ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in lungs harvested on day 15. (B) Mtb CFUs from mLNs of mice harvested on day 12. (C) CCR2-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11 and received either MHCII WT or MHCII KO IMs on days 8 and 10. Flow cytometry was performed on lungs harvested on day 15. (D) zDC-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and cDCs were depleted on day 7, 9 and 11, and the number of ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells was determined in mLNs harvested on day 12. (E) The number of CFU in mLNs of PBS and DT treated zDC-DTR mice. (F) FLT3LKO mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and lungs were harvested on day 15 to quantify the ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells. Each dot represents an individual mouse. Error bars denote SEM. Data are representative of two independent experiments.

![Figure 4—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig4-figsupp1-v1.jpg)

**Figure 4—figure supplement 1.:** MHC class II KO/CCR2-DTR mice infected with Mtb and depleted on days 7, 9, and 11 received a dose of purified IMs on days 8 and 10 and were harvested on day 12 when the total number of transferred IMs per mLN was quantified. Each group contains five mice. Data are representative of two independent experiments.

![Figure 4—figure supplement 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig4-figsupp2-v1.jpg)

**Figure 4—figure supplement 2.:** zDC-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and cDCs were depleted on days 7, 9 and 11. On day 12 mLNs were harvested to quantify the number of ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells. Data are representative of two independent experiments containing four mice per group.

![Figure 4—figure supplement 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig4-figsupp3-v1.jpg)

**Figure 4—figure supplement 3.:** FLT3LKO mice were infected with Mtb and mLNs were harvested on day 12 for CFU analysis. Each dot represents an individual mouse. Data are representative of two independent experiments.

Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46, whereas IMs do not. To determine whether classical DCs are required for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming, we used zDC-DTR mice, in which DT administration leads to a loss of classical DC populations (Meredith et al., 2012a; Meredith et al., 2012b). We transferred C7 T cells into zDC-DTR mice, infected the mice with Mtb and administered DT on days 7–11 following infection. Depletion of classical DCs resulted in markedly reduced C7 T cell expansion (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) but did not reduce the number of live Mtb in mLNs (Figure 4E). FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs, also have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection (Figure 4F) despite the presence of Mtb in the mLN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). These results indicate that classical DCs, while dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs, are essential for CD4 T cell priming.

These experiments have refined our understanding of the role of IMs during the initiation of adaptive immune defense against M. tuberculosis infection. During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs, an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming. Our results extend previous reports that IMs influence CD4 T cell priming (Leon et al., 2007; Hohl et al., 2009; Nakano et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011) by demonstrating that IMs serve as transporters of live bacteria from the site of infection to the site of T cell priming.

In contrast to reports from other disease models demonstrating that IMs differentiate into DCs and then directly prime CD4 T cells (Cheong et al., 2010; Zigmond et al., 2012) our adoptive transfer studies using MHC class II KO mice reveal that IMs, despite acquiring characteristics of DCs, do not prime Mtb-specific CD4 T cells in vivo. Why IMs fail to prime DCs in this setting remains unclear. Evidence that moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses suggests that IMs can process and present antigen (Schreurs et al., 1999). Recovery of several hundred adoptively transferred IMs from the mLNs of infected mice also suggests that sufficient numbers of IM were present to prime T cells. One possible explanation is that IMs, by virtue of being infected with Mtb, are ineffective at stimulating Mtb-specific lymphocytes, in contrast to resident dendritic cells that have not been infected (Wolf et al., 2007).

Antigen transport and T cell priming are often considered the two major functions of DCs. A number of studies, however, have demonstrated that multiple DC subsets can be involved in priming of naive T cells (Itano et al., 2003). Other studies characterizing CD8 T cell responses to cutaneous viral infection have demonstrated a role for CD103+ DCs in transport and priming with potential contributions by inflammatory monocytes (Bedoui et al., 2009; Edismo et al., 2009). One previous study has suggested that IMs carry fungal antigens from a site of cutaneous inoculation to draining LNs and transfer antigens to LN resident DCs (Ersland et al., 2010). Our study extends this finding to live pulmonary infection with Mtb. IMs transport bacteria to lymph nodes and transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells prior to CD4 T cell priming.

The mechanism of antigen transfer in mLNs remains undefined. It is possible that cross-dressing (Wakim et al., 2011), in which infected cells pass MHC molecules to uninfected cells, plays a role during Mtb infection. We did not detect transfer of MHC class II molecules from host cells to adoptively transferred, MHC class II-deficient monocytes. The number of MHC/peptide complexes required per APC to stimulate T cell responses, however, may be very small and below our level of detection. That said, given our finding that MHC class II-deficient IMs effectively complemented monocyte-depleted, MHC class II sufficient mice while MHC class II-expressing monocytes could not correct deficient T cell priming in MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted mice, we believe that transfer of MHC class II molecules in either direction plays a minimal role in T cell priming during Mtb infection. Future studies will determine whether live Mtb are transferred to classical DCs, or whether transfer principally involves the movement of processed or unprocessed proteins from infected monocytes to uninfected DCs.

## Materials and methods

### Mice

C57BL/6 and MHC class II-deficient mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory. The generation of ESAT-6-specific C7 TCR transgenic, CCR2-DTR, CCR2-GFP and zDC-DTR mice were previously described (Wolf et al., 2007; Gallegos et al., 2008; Hohl et al., 2009). For depletion experiments, mice were injected i.p. with 20 ng/g body weight DT. All mice were bred and maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Research Animal Resource Center. Sex-and age-matched controls were used in all experiments according to institutional guidelines for animal care. All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center.

### Aerosol infections with M. tuberculosis

M. tuberculosis Erdman was grown in 7H9 media, and log phase cultures were diluted to 8 × 106 bacilli per millimeter and sonicated before infection with an aerosol exposure system (Glass-Col). The volume of suspension, and exposure time were calibrated to deliver ∼100 CFU per animal. To determine infection dose, three mice were killed 1 day after infection and lungs were homogenized in PBS/0.05% Tween-80, and half the lung homogenate was plated. At various intervals after infection the left lung was harvested from individual mice and homogenized in PBS/0.05% Tween-80. Serial dilutions were made in PBS/0.05% Tween-80 and plated onto Middlebrook 7H10 agar (BD Biosciences). After 3 weeks of incubation at 37°C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere, colonies were counted.

### Adoptive IM transfer

Inflammatory monocytes were harvested from the bone marrow of CCR2-GFP mice. CD4 T cells and NK+ cells were removed using antibody depletion kits from Miltenyi Biotec. The remaining cells were then stained with anti FLT3 PE and anti C-kit PE antibodies and EGFP+, PE- cells were sorted by the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center flow cytometry core facility. The cells were re-suspended in PBS and 2 × 10 (Kipnis et al., 2003) cells per mouse were injected via the tail vein.

### Statistics

All data are presented as the arithmetic mean ± SEM. Statistical validation was done with the Student’s t test. p<0.05 were considered significant, p>0.05 were considered insignificant.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.01086.012](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.01086.012)

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for sending your work entitled “Essential yet limited role for CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes during Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific T cell priming” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by a Senior editor and 2 reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The Reviewing editor and the other reviewer discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

This is an elegant and straightforward study that makes an important contribution on the role of different APCs in transport and presentation of antigen in vivo in a biologically relevant system.

The only open aspect is the mechanism of antigen transfer from inflammatory monocytes to resident DC. It would be interesting if the authors could provide insights on why the monocytes that carry Mtb to lymph nodes do not present antigen to CD4+ T cells. Is there a problem with their localization within lymph nodes? Or are they incompetent for antigen processing and presentation (their antigen presentation capacity could be tested ex vivo)? Or are they too few to function as APC and their role is limited to spreading a live organism? In addition the authors may also consider the alternative possibility that resident DCs transfer their MHC class II molecules to inflammatory monocytes (a process related to “cross dressing”). In this case DC depletion would block T cell activation because the source of MHC class II is absent. This possibility could be addressed by asking whether there is any MHC class II on class II KO inflammatory monocytes after adoptive transfer and infection. While these experiments would provide a mechanistic explanation to the results, they are not essential to support the major conclusions of the study and consequently the authors may address these issues in the Discussion.

results.result: CCR2-expressing cells are not required for establishment of pulmonary Mtb infection. Using CCR2-DTR mice, the authors show that DT administration depletes inflammatory monocytes from lung and mLN (C22), and that depletion around the time of aerosol infection does not affect mycobacterial growth in lungs (C23), leading to the conclusion that CCR2-expressing cells are dispensable for initial infection establishment (C24).
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The depletion strategy is clearly described (C21), depletion is confirmed by flow cytometry (C22), and CFU data demonstrate no difference in lung bacterial burden (C23), justifying the inference in C24.

results.result: Transient depletion of CCR2-expressing cells during days 7-11 post-infection prevents Mtb delivery to mediastinal lymph nodes. Depletion during this window resulted in increased lung CFUs by day 15 (C26), but at day 12, lung CFUs were similar between depleted and control mice (C27) while mLN CFUs were markedly reduced in depleted mice (C28), demonstrating that monocyte depletion specifically impairs bacterial transport to lymph nodes (C3).
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are directly supported by CFU data in Figures 1B-D. The temporal dissociation between lung and lymph node bacterial burden strongly supports the conclusion that CCR2+ cells are required for Mtb transport to draining lymph nodes during this specific time window.

results.result: Monocyte depletion during days 7-11 post-infection impairs CD4 T cell priming in mediastinal lymph nodes. The authors hypothesized that reduced Mtb transport would delay T cell priming (C29), and demonstrated that monocyte-depleted mice had smaller mLNs with reduced CD4 T cell numbers (C30), failed C7 T cell proliferation in mLNs at day 12 (C31), and reduced C7 T cell frequencies in lungs at day 21 (C32), confirming that monocyte depletion reduces CD4 T cell responses (C4).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 are well-supported by data in Figure 2A-D using adoptively transferred TCR transgenic T cells as a readout. The experimental design appropriately links impaired bacterial transport (previous result) to defective T cell priming. C29 is appropriately labeled as a hypothesis/reasoning step.

results.result: Supplementing the endogenous T cell repertoire with naive ESAT-6-specific CD4 T cells enhances immune defense, but this protection requires monocytes. Transfer of naive C7 T cells reduced lung Mtb CFUs 4-5 fold (C33), suggesting enhanced immune defense (C34), but monocyte depletion abrogated this protection (C35).
results.evaluation: Claims C33 and C35 are directly supported by CFU data in Figure 2E. The inference in C34 is reasonable given the reduced bacterial burden. This result demonstrates the functional importance of the monocyte-dependent T cell priming pathway.

results.result: Highly purified inflammatory monocytes can restore Mtb transport to lymph nodes and rescue T cell priming in monocyte-depleted mice. IMs were purified to >99% purity by excluding other CCR2-expressing cell types (C37), trafficked to lungs and mLNs (C38), underwent phenotypic changes during migration including downregulation of CCR2/CD11b and upregulation of MHC-II/CD11c/CD103 (C39-C40), restored Mtb delivery to mLNs (C41), and rescued C7 T cell priming (C44).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C44 are well-supported by data in Figure 3 and supplements. The purification strategy is rigorous (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), phenotypic tracking is shown (Figure 3A-B), and functional rescue is demonstrated for both bacterial transport (Figure 3C) and T cell priming (Figure 3D-E). This confirms that IMs specifically are responsible for the observed effects.

results.result: Inflammatory monocytes are not limiting during the first two weeks of Mtb infection. Infusion of additional IMs to wild-type mice did not enhance Mtb delivery to mLNs (C42), suggesting endogenous IMs are sufficient during this period (C43).
results.evaluation: Claim C42 is stated as an experimental observation, and C43 is a reasonable inference. This control experiment strengthens the interpretation that the rescue effects observed in depleted mice reflect restoration of a necessary function rather than pharmacological enhancement.

results.result: CCR2 signaling is not required for trafficking of inflammatory monocytes from infected lungs to mediastinal lymph nodes. Wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs (C45), indicating CCR2 signaling does not contribute to this trafficking step (C46).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by data in Figure 3F showing equivalent CFU delivery by WT and CCR2-KO monocytes. This is an important mechanistic finding distinguishing CCR2's role in bone marrow egress from its role (or lack thereof) in lung-to-lymph node trafficking.

results.result: Inflammatory monocytes serve as carriers of Mtb to lymph nodes but do not directly prime CD4 T cells. Transfer of MHC-II+ IMs to MHC-II-deficient recipients restored Mtb transport (C5, C48-C49) but failed to enable T cell priming (C6, C47). Conversely, transfer of MHC-II-deficient IMs to MHC-II+ recipients rescued T cell priming (C7, C50). Together, these experiments demonstrate that IMs function primarily as bacterial carriers, enabling but not directly mediating CD4 T cell priming (C51).
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 and C47-C50 are well-supported by the elegant reciprocal adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 4A-C. The experimental logic is sound: if IMs directly primed T cells, MHC-II+ IMs should rescue priming in MHC-II-deficient hosts, but they do not. The conclusion in C51 is strongly supported by this data.

results.result: Classical dendritic cells are dispensable for Mtb transport to lymph nodes but required for CD4 T cell priming. Specific depletion of cDCs using zDC-DTR mice did not reduce Mtb delivery to mLNs (C8, C55) but markedly reduced C7 T cell expansion (C9, C54).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C54-C55 are supported by data in Figure 4D-E using zDC-DTR mice. This result provides a clear functional distinction between IMs (required for transport) and cDCs (required for priming), complementing the MHC-II transfer experiments.

results.result: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but retain inflammatory monocytes, have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses despite presence of Mtb in lymph nodes. FLT3L-KO mice showed reduced CD4 T cell responses (C57) despite Mtb presence in mLNs (C58), confirming that cDCs are essential for T cell priming (C60) but dispensable for bacterial trafficking (C59).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 are supported by data in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 3. This genetic model provides independent confirmation of the cDC depletion results, strengthening the conclusion about the distinct roles of IMs and cDCs.

results.result: During the second week of Mtb infection, inflammatory monocytes transport bacteria to lymph nodes and transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells, which then prime CD4 T cells. IMs acquire DC characteristics during trafficking (C10) but do not directly prime T cells (C11, C64). Instead, IMs play the critical role of delivering Mtb to draining lymph nodes (C61), an indispensable step for T cell priming (C62), serving as transporters from infection site to priming site (C63, C71).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C61-C64 represent the major conclusions of the manuscript, synthesizing results from multiple experimental approaches. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective evidence from depletion, adoptive transfer, and genetic models. The model of IM-to-cDC antigen transfer is strongly supported though the precise mechanism remains undefined.

results.result: Transfer of MHC class II molecules plays a minimal role in T cell priming during Mtb infection. The authors did not detect MHC-II transfer from host cells to adoptively transferred MHC-II-deficient monocytes (C73), though acknowledge detection limits (C74). Based on the reciprocal transfer experiments, they conclude MHC-II transfer in either direction plays minimal role (C75).
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is an experimental observation, C74 acknowledges technical limitations, and C75 is a reasonable inference based on the functional data from reciprocal transfers (C5-C7). While cross-dressing cannot be completely ruled out, the functional evidence argues against it being the primary mechanism.

results.result: Background knowledge and prior work establish the context for the study. These claims summarize established knowledge about CD4 T cells in Mtb defense (C1), IM phenotype and function (C2, C12-C18), limitations of CCR2-deficient mice (C19-C20), timing of T cell priming (C25), CCR2 expression patterns (C36), DC markers (C52-C53, C56), and prior studies on monocyte and DC roles in T cell priming (C14-C15, C65, C68-C70).
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately cite prior literature and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide necessary context for interpreting the current study's findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Speculative explanations and future directions. The authors propose that IMs infected with Mtb may be ineffective at stimulating T cells (C67), suggest cross-dressing might play a role (C72), and identify future studies needed to determine the mechanism of antigen transfer (C76).
results.evaluation: These claims are explicitly speculative (C67, C72) or describe future work (C76). They represent reasonable hypotheses based on the data but are not tested in the current study. C67 is appropriately cited to prior work showing infected DCs are poor stimulators.

results.result: Transient depletion of inflammatory monocytes (IMs) during days 7-11 post-infection prevents Mtb delivery to mediastinal lymph nodes (mLNs), reduces CD4 T cell priming in the mLNs, and results in reduced CD4 T cell frequencies in the lungs. This demonstrates that IMs play a critical role in delivering live Mtb to draining lymph nodes, which is essential for CD4 T cell priming.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the study as 'elegant and straightforward' and state it 'makes an important contribution on the role of different APCs in transport and presentation of antigen in vivo.' The reviewers do not challenge these core findings about IM depletion effects on bacterial transport and T cell priming, accepting them as the foundation for the study's conclusions.

results.result: Adoptive transfer of highly purified IMs (>99% pure) to monocyte-depleted mice restores Mtb transport to mLNs and rescues CD4 T cell priming. Transferred IMs traffic from lung to mLNs while acquiring DC characteristics (downregulating CCR2/CD11b, upregulating MHC II/CD11c/CD103), and this trafficking does not require CCR2 signaling. This demonstrates that IMs serve as transporters of live bacteria from the infection site to the T cell priming site.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge these findings as part of the study's 'important contribution' on APC roles in antigen transport. The adoptive transfer experiments are not questioned and form the basis for the reviewers' discussion about mechanisms of antigen transfer from IMs to resident DCs.

results.result: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient recipients restores Mtb transport but does not enable CD4 T cell priming, while transfer of MHC class II-deficient IMs to MHC class II-expressing recipients corrects CD4 T cell priming. This demonstrates that IMs primarily serve as carriers of Mtb, delivering bacteria to mLNs and enabling but not directly priming CD4 T cells, with antigen transfer to classical DCs occurring prior to T cell priming.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as supporting the major conclusions, stating the study demonstrates 'the role of different APCs in transport and presentation of antigen.' The reviewers request mechanistic insights about why monocytes don't present antigen, but do not challenge the experimental findings themselves.

results.result: Specific depletion of classical DCs (using zDC-DTR mice) or genetic deficiency of classical DCs (FLT3L-deficient mice) markedly reduces CD4 T cell priming but does not reduce Mtb delivery to mLNs. This demonstrates that classical DCs are dispensable for bacterial trafficking but essential for CD4 T cell priming during Mtb infection.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these findings and accept them as part of the study's demonstration of distinct roles for different APC populations. The complementary roles of IMs (transport) versus classical DCs (priming) form a core conclusion that reviewers describe as an 'important contribution.'

results.result: Although IMs acquire characteristics of DCs while delivering Mtb to lymph nodes, classical DCs (cDCs) but not monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs) induce proliferation of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this conclusion as a primary finding of the study. They request mechanistic insights about why monocytes that acquire DC characteristics still fail to prime T cells, but do not challenge the finding itself, treating it as an established result requiring explanation.

results.result: The authors propose several speculative mechanisms for why IMs fail to prime T cells despite acquiring DC characteristics, including that infected IMs may be ineffective at stimulating lymphocytes, that cross-dressing may play a role, and that MHC class II transfer may occur below detection levels. The authors did not detect MHC class II transfer from host cells to adoptively transferred MHC class II-deficient monocytes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly identify the mechanism of antigen transfer as 'the only open aspect' and request insights on why monocytes don't present antigen. They suggest testing whether there is MHC class II on class II KO inflammatory monocytes after transfer (cross-dressing), but note 'these experiments would provide a mechanistic explanation to the results, they are not essential to support the major conclusions.'

results.result: Transfer of naïve ESAT-6-specific CD4 T cells (C7 T cells) to control mice resulted in enhanced protection (4-5 fold reduction in Mtb CFUs), suggesting that supplementing the endogenous T cell repertoire enhances immune defense. Monocyte depletion abrogated this enhanced protection.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these findings, which serve as supporting evidence for the importance of monocyte-mediated T cell priming. The results are consistent with the overall narrative that reviewers describe as 'elegant and straightforward.'

results.result: CCR2-DTR mice that received DT surrounding the time of aerosol infection did not differ from control mice in mycobacterial growth in lungs, indicating that CCR2-expressing cells are not required for establishment of pulmonary infection following Mtb inhalation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding, which establishes that the effects of monocyte depletion are specific to later stages of infection rather than initial establishment. This supports the temporal specificity of the study's main conclusions.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about Mtb immunity, inflammatory monocyte characteristics, CCR2 function, prior studies implicating IMs in CD4 T cell responses, limitations of CCR2-deficient mice, timing of CD4 T cell priming, and prior studies on DC subsets and antigen transfer in other infection models.
results.evaluation: These are background claims supported by citations that provide context for the study. Reviewers do not question these established facts, which frame the study's rationale and significance.

results.result: Methodological claims about the experimental approach: CCR2-DTR mice were used to transiently deplete IMs, DT administration depletes inflammatory monocytes from lung and mLN, and infusion of IMs to WT mice did not enhance Mtb delivery to mLNs, suggesting IMs are not limiting during the first 2 weeks of infection.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the experimental methodology or these supporting observations. The CCR2-DTR system is accepted as appropriate for addressing the study's questions about temporal roles of monocytes.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C33-C35 regarding functional importance of monocyte-dependent T cell priming pathway. Both evaluations find these claims supported by CFU data in Figure 2E.

Strong agreement on background/contextual claims (C1-C2, C12-C20, C25, C36, C52-C53, C56, C65, C68-C70). Both evaluations accept these as appropriately cited established knowledge providing necessary context.

Strong agreement on reciprocal MHC-II transfer experiments (C5-C7, C47-C51). Both find these claims well-supported and accept the conclusion that IMs do not directly prime T cells. Peer reviewers request mechanistic insights but do not challenge the findings.

Strong agreement on IM purification and adoptive transfer experiments (C37-C41, C44). Both evaluations accept these as demonstrating IMs are specifically responsible for bacterial transport and T cell priming effects. OpenEval also includes C45-C46 about CCR2-independent trafficking.

Agreement on uncertain/speculative nature of mechanistic claims (C67, C72, C76). Both evaluations recognize these as hypotheses or future work rather than tested conclusions. Peer reviewers identify mechanism of antigen transfer as 'the only open aspect.'

Agreement on claims C23-C24 regarding no difference in lung bacterial burden during early infection. Both accept this as establishing temporal specificity of monocyte effects. OpenEval also covers depletion methodology (C21-C22).

Agreement on control experiment claims C42-C43 showing adoptive transfer into WT mice has no effect. Both accept this as strengthening interpretation of rescue experiments. Peer review also covers depletion methodology (C21-C22).

Agreement on temporal dissociation between lung and lymph node bacterial burden (C26-C28, C3). Both find these claims supported by CFU data. Peer review groups these with broader conclusions about T cell priming (C29-C32, C61-C62).

Agreement on T cell priming defects following impaired bacterial transport (C29-C32, C4). Both evaluations accept these claims as supported by adoptive transfer of TCR transgenic T cells. Peer review groups with broader study conclusions.

Agreement on cDC depletion experiments using Batf3-KO mice (C56-C60). Both accept these as providing independent confirmation of distinct IM and cDC roles. Peer review groups with zDC-DTR depletion results (C8, C54-C55).

Agreement on zDC-DTR cDC depletion experiments (C8, C54-C55). Both find these supported and demonstrating functional distinction between IMs and cDCs. Peer review groups with Batf3-KO results (C57-C60).

Agreement on major conclusions (C10-C11) about distinct roles of IMs and cDCs. Both evaluations accept these as primary findings. OpenEval includes broader synthesis (C61-C64, C71) while peer reviewers request mechanistic insights without challenging findings.

Agreement on CCR2-independent trafficking of IMs from lung to lymph node (C45-C46). Both accept this mechanistic finding. Peer review groups with broader IM adoptive transfer results (C37-C41, C44, C63).

Partial overlap on mechanistic uncertainty. OpenEval addresses cross-dressing evidence (C73-C75) as supported inference against this mechanism. Peer review identifies mechanism as uncertain and suggests testing cross-dressing (C67, C72-C74, C76).
